newsitem.title: UGANDA: Ugandan rebels are obscure newcomers to conflict.
newsitem.headline: Ugandan rebels are obscure newcomers to conflict.

text.p: The Ugandan rebels attacking western Uganda from Zaire are relative newcomers in a confusing patchwork of armed groups ravaging the region.
Ugandans say the rebels, known as the Allied Democratic Force (ADF), are mainly Moslems from northern Uganda and depend on support from the Islamist government in Khartoum.
They are not to be confused with the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), the much larger Zairean rebel group which now controls much of eastern Zaire.

"We first heard of them a couple of months ago," said Wafula Ogutu, editor of the independent newspaper The Monitor. "We don't know them or their leadership at all. The apparent link is Allah. The link is in Sudan," he added.
The rebels made their first big attack in the middle of November, soon after the Zairean rebels routed Zairean government troops in the east of the country.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni said then that Ugandan troops had killed 230 of them and captured 30.
In the fighting this week, Ugandan officers say their troops have killed about 50 of the rebels.

Despite the scale of the fighting, Museveni and his commanders have played down the significance of the attacks from the west and they continue to emphasise the chronic threat from the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) in the north of the country.
The LRA, a Christian fundamentalist group also allegedly backed by Sudan, operates well inside Uganda, among the Acholi people around the northern districts of Gulu, Lira and Kitgum.
The Ugandan army commander, Major-General Mugisha Muntu, said this week that the army could annihilate the rebels in the southwest and restore calm and security there.
Muntu told a parliamentary committee that the only real security problem remained the LRA, led by Joseph Kony, who wants to rule Uganda in accordance with the Ten Commandments.
"There is also an external factor. Sudan (is) replenishing the rebels whenever we defeat them and is also giving them bases for training," Muntu said in sworn testimony.
Museveni has camped in the northern town of Gulu in the last few weeks, as part of a promise to Ugandans that he will personally direct fighting against the LRA.

Despite coming under pressure from Ugandan politicians and Acholi elders to negotiate with Kony, Museveni says he prefers a military solution to a conflict threatening to reverse economic gains achieved by his government since 1986.
On the army's control over the borders, Muntu said: "There is only one border which is still a problem: Sudan."
One independent analyst said the Ugandan government was right in saying the Zairean government, which has little control outside towns, had nothing to do with the ADF rebels.

"I don't think Zaireans are involved with them at all. But by operating from there, they can do anything they like and stir up trouble for Uganda," he said. "Zaire is not in a position to coordinate the war against Uganda."
Asked how serious the threat was, he said: "The western one will be defeated much more easily than the northern one."
